## Problem 1 (P1)
### P1 Setup
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
library(tidyverse)

data("ny_noaa")
```
### P1 Description
```{r Description}

str(ny_noaa)
summary(ny_noaa)
ny_noaa |> summarize(across(everything(), \(x) mean(is.na(x))))
```
The `ny_noaa` dataset has `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns, with weather records from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` stations across New York State from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` and `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Each row is one day of weather at one station. The columns are the station ID, the dare, how much it rained, how much it snowed, how deep the snow on the ground was, and the highest and lowest temperatures of the day. The temperatures are saved as text
instead of numbers, so they need to be converted before we can use them.

A lot of data is missing. The temperature columns have the most gaps, with 1,134,358 days missing `tmax` and 1,134,420 missing `tmin`, which is close to half the dataset. Snow depth is missing for 591,786 days, snowfall for 381,221, and rain for 145,838. This is probably because many stations only measure rain and snow, not temperature. There are also a few values that don't make sense, like negative snowfall and record days with impossibly large amounts of rain and snow, which are probably recording mistakes.

### P1a
```{r Question 1a}
ny_noaa_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
#I split the date here into year, month, and days columns
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |> #This part converts the temperature into numbers and changes tenth of Celcius to Celcius and rainfall into milimiters, instead of tenths. Did not do this for snowfall and depth, since they are in reasonable units.
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
#Given that I understand these measures in inches better, I turned them into that measure with this code, making them more reasonable for the average person.
    prcp = prcp / 10 / 25.4,
    snow = snow / 25.4,
    snwd = snwd / 25.4
  )
# This part of the code will let me see the most common values for snow
ny_noaa_df |> 
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```
The most common values are 0 and NA, indicating that most days either had no snowfall or had missing snowfall data. The next most frequent numerical values are 0.98, 0.51, and 2.01 inches, corresponding to approximately 1, 0.5, and 2 inches of snowfall, respectively. This suggest that snowfall commonly occurs in small amoutns.

### P1b
#### P1b Setup
```{r Question 1b Setup}
## Set the size of figures created by R and how they appear in the document
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

## Set a default theme for all plots
theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```
#### P1b Plot Chunk
```{r Question 1b Plot Chunk}
ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_when(
      month == 1 ~ "January",
      month == 7 ~ "July"
    )) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .3) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .3) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature in January and July by station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average max temperature (°C)"
  )
```

January is much colder than July. Most stations have average temperatures between -5 and 5 °C in January, compared with 25 to 30 C in July. January temperatures also vary more from year to year, ranging from around -10 to 10 C, while July temperatures stay within a narrower range.

A few values stand out as outliers. The most noticeble is a station in July late 1980's with an average temperature of about 14 Celcius, much lower than the other stations that month. January also has a couple of unusually low averages, including about -13 C in early 1980's and -12 C in the midd 200's.

### P1c
```{r question_1c, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 1.8}
# for Panel 1, a scatterplot would overplot millions of points, so geom_hex() is used instead as it groups points into hexagons and colors each one by how many points it contains.
tmax_tmin_p = 
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    title = "Max vs. min temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")  # move the count legend to the side so its numbers don't overlap

## For panel 2, Snowfall is in inches, so 100 mm is converted to inches (100 / 25.4) for the filter.
## factor(year) treats each year as its own category, giving one ridge per year.
library(ggridges)

snow_p = 
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100 / 25.4) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) + 
  scale_y_discrete(breaks = c("1981", "1985", "1990", "1995", "2000", "2005", "2010")) +  # label every 5 years
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall by year (0–100 mm, shown in inches)",
    x = "Snowfall (in)",
    y = "Year"
  )

## Combine the two plots into one figure, stacked vertically with "/"
library(patchwork)

tmax_tmin_p / snow_p + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 2))
```

## Problem 2 (P2)

### P2 load, tidy, merge, and organize
```{r Problem 2}
covar_df = 
# Imports the data and skips the lines with notes
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
# Removes participants under 21
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
# Removes any missing data
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex == 1 ~ "male",
      sex == 2 ~ "female"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    education = case_when(
      education == 1 ~ "Less than high school",
      education == 2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      education == 3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")
    )
  )
# Imports accelometer data 
accel_df = 
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

# Merges data by ID of the participants
nhanes_df = 
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")
```
### P2 reader friendly table + Age Dist. Visualization
```{r P2 reader friendly table}
covar_df |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education", "Men", "Women")
    
## Age distribution visualization
  )
covar_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by education and sex",
    x = "Education",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```

About half of the participants without missing demographic data have more than a high school education, for both men and women. The less than high school group is fairly evenly split between men and women. Lastly, the high school equivalent group has more men than women.

Looking at the age distributions, people with less than a high school education have a median age of around 60, with little difference between men and women. In the high school equivalent group, women are noticeably older than men, with a median age of around 60 compared with the early 50s for men. In the more than high school group, men and women have similar age distributions, with men slightly older (mid 40s) than women (early 40s). This group is also the youngest overall.

### P2 total activity variable + Plot
```{r P2 total activty}
#This adds up the activity for all of the participants
total_activity_df = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims))
```
```{r Plot}
# This one plots activity against age with men and women
total_activity_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .5) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

In all of the groups the total activity tends to decrease with age. For those with less than high school we see a spike in their 60's bigger for males. Those with high school equivalent we see a spike in their 40s bigger for females, and a smaller spike in their 70 only observable for females, though females in general have a higher actvity. Among those with more than high school the activity is more constant, with males showing a small spike in thier 50's and females in their 60's, though similarly to the previous one, females have an overall higher activity. 

### P2 24-hour activity time course
```{r 24 hours}
nhanes_df |> 
## Changes minutes to hours
  mutate(hour = minute / 60) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_line(aes(group = seqn), alpha = .1) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24)) + 
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity by education and sex",
    x = "Hour of the day",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

This shows that from midnight to 6am, most people show no activity. However, regardless of sex or education, the activity levels seem to go up from 6am to noon, then plateau, and then 7pm they drop. Though, females do show slightly more activity than men in those with more than hs education. 

## Problem 3 (P3)
